summary: Weekly sync focused on balancing TTFT and streaming latency across sequence lengths and kernel choices. Decided to run hedging microburst experiments, collect live seq-length distribution from Argentum, and explore Dedicated burst vs hosted fallback policy. Security/KMS question flagged for follow-up.
topics: TTFT behavior with streaming and early token paths
Dedicated vs Hosted fallback policies and cost implications
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Lucas and Ruth from our side. How are we doing in Argentum?
[00:07] Priya (Argentum): Hi, Priya here, Daniel and Emma on. We're good, busy week.
[00:12] Maya: Cool. Goal for today is to go through the last run's TTFT numbers, confirm the small hedging experiment, and agree next steps.
[00:22] Lucas: I'll start with the numbers I ran Tuesday — I re-ran the streaming tests with the sequence length buckets Priya sent last week, but I used two kernel configs: the fused-attn path and the fallback cuBLAS-ish path. The fused path gave lower 50p on token 1 but higher variance on 99p when we simulated bursts.
[00:40] Priya: When you say fused path, is that the one that uses the newer attention kernel we demoed? The one that broke down at long seqlens last time?
[00:47] Lucas: Yeah, that's the one — it's optimized for short prefix and smaller KV cache pressure, so TTFT for short outputs is very good. But when we pushed sequences to 512 the kernel's memory access pattern caused jitter; we saw microbursts where single-request latency spiked up.
[01:05] Daniel: Just to clarify, our user workload is mostly 30 to 80 tokens but 5% of requests go to 250–600 tokens for document completions. We care about 95p being under 350ms and 99p under 700ms for chat flows.
[01:24] Maya: Good — that helps. We should tune for the 95p target while keeping TTFT low for the common short cases. That’s where hedging comes in.
[01:32] Emma: Hedging meaning parallel fallbacks? I thought hedging increased cost a lot.
[01:36] Lucas: It can but our microburst hedging design tries to minimize extra tokens — we open a lightweight fast-path estimate and only fully route if it looks like the request needs more compute. There's also early-stop heuristics on the prefix. In tests, average cost delta was ~6% but 99p improved from 950ms to 520ms for one config.
[01:56] Priya: That's promising. Did you test with streaming enabled? Our UI relies on steady early tokens showing up.
[02:02] Lucas: Yes, streaming was on. The tricky bit is the streaming handshake — the first-stream chunk latency is highly sensitive to kernel startup. The fused kernel gives faster first-chunk for seqlen<128 but when you have KV cache misses it slows. We saw the fallback kernel (more conservative) had slightly higher median TTFT but much better 99p stability.
[02:24] Maya: So tradeoff: fused = low TTFT median; fallback = predictable tail. For Argentum, with 95p target, fallback might be safer for mixed seqlen traffic unless we do hedging.
[02:36] Omar (Argentum): Quick question — is the KV cache warm across sessions in your tests? Our usage pattern often hits cold-cache due to multi-tenant routing.
[02:45] Lucas: Good point. I ran both warm and cold scenarios. Cold cache exacerbates the fused kernel jitter. Warm cache reduces tail by ~20%.
[02:53] Daniel: Our infra will likely cause cold cache frequently; we have aggressive autoscaling.
[02:57] Lucas: Right, so hedging becomes more attractive.
[03:02] Ruth (Redwood CSM): We also shared a doc in the deck folder called "hedge-options.pdf" — link in the notes.
[03:08] Maya: Let's look at specific experiments — Lucas, can you summarize the three kernel configs you'll run and what metrics you'll post?
[03:14] Lucas: Sure: Config A = fused-attn high-perf with streaming enabled, no hedging; Config B = fallback-conservative kernel with streaming; Config C = fused-attn + hedging (light probe to fallback after 80ms). For each I'll capture TTFT median/95/99, per-token cost delta, and first-stream-chunk latency. I'll also capture CPU/GPU utilization traces and KV cache hit rates.
[03:39] Priya: For the histograms, can you bucket by request seqlen ranges that match our production histogram? I can export exact buckets.
[03:45] Lucas: Absolutely — please share the CSV.
[03:47] Priya: I'll put it in the project folder after this call.
[03:50] Emma: Also, regarding Dedicated vs Hosted: we want the option to reserve capacity for peak windows. How does that interact with the hedging?
[03:59] Maya: Dedicated gives you much tighter control of cold cache and reduced noisy neighbor jitter. That means fused-attn becomes more stable in Dedicated, so you can keep low TTFT and low tail. Hosted fallback policies can still route to a Dedicated pool or a cheaper variant when needed. Cost-wise Dedicated has a baseline commitment but lower per-token variance.
[04:18] Daniel: So maybe the path is: start with Hosted with hedging while we gather seq-length distribution and then move to a small Dedicated pool for peak hours.
[04:26] Maya: That’s what a few customers have done. We'll provide cost models for both choices.
[04:30] Priya: About security — we had a flag in the RFP around KMS and audit logs. Any blockers there?
[04:36] Maya: We can support customer-managed KMS with Private deployment or Dedicated with a managed KMS integration. Audit logs and token-level tracing are available; we'll share the SOC2/ISO snippets. Lucas, can you join the security deep-dive?
[04:47] Lucas: Yep, happy to.
[04:49] Priya: Great. Back to hedging: we need clear cost estimates. Can you quantify the 6% cost delta you mentioned — is that for median or for worst-case?
[04:58] Lucas: That's average cost across mixed traffic in our sim; the worst-case delta when you always trigger fallback is higher, around 18–22%. But real workloads rarely trigger full fallback. With an 80ms probe threshold tuned to your seqlen buckets we saw ~5–8% cost in most runs.
[05:20] Emma: If we move to Dedicated could hedging be disabled?
[05:24] Lucas: You could reduce hedging or widen the probe threshold in Dedicated; because latency variance is lower, hedging can be less aggressive.
[05:31] Priya: Let's talk measurements — please include TTFT microsecond granularity if possible and also the stream chunk timings.
[05:38] Lucas: Will do. Also I'll attach traces showing GPU kernel startup time and small flame charts.
[05:43] Maya: Anything else on kernels? We noticed last week a memory growth pattern on the fused kernel with long sequences.
[05:50] Lucas: Yes, there's a leaking path if the trading between KV slices isn't trimmed — we patched in a test branch but not mainline. The memory growth appears only at seqlen>1024. For your 600 max we didn't see catastrophic growth, but it's worth validating.
[06:05] Omar: Our maximum is 600, but occasional recall jobs can spike. Could we set a per-request hard cap to avoid kernel mem growth?
[06:12] Lucas: Yep, we can configure per-request seqlen cap and fallback to a safer kernel when it hits cap.
[06:18] Priya: For the experiment, can we have one run where requests >400 get forced fallback so we can see the hybrid behavior?
[06:24] Lucas: Yes I'll include a hybrid run.
[06:27] Maya: Great. Now quick recap of decisions so far — run A/B/C as Lucas described, Priya to send CSV seq-length buckets, Maya to email pricing, security deep-dive to be scheduled. Any blockers?
[06:39] Emma: One thing — competitors. We did a quick bench with another vendor and saw lower medians but similar tails. Any pointers for comparing apples to apples?
[06:48] Maya: Ask for the same load shapes and warm/cold cache conditions. We'll share our runner scripts if helpful.
[06:54] Ruth: I'll drop the runner scripts and the hedging experiment template in the shared folder after call.
[07:00] Daniel: Sounds good. Also, about monitoring — we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route SLA dashboards. Can Redwood's console show per-route 95/99 token latency with alerting?
[07:12] Lucas: Yes, Console exposes per-route token-level breakdowns and you can set alerts on 95/99 percentiles and cost per route. We'll demo that in the next call if you want.
[07:21] Priya: Please do. That will help our SRE to validate.
[07:25] Maya: All right last housekeeping — timeline. Lucas: run experiments and post results by Wednesday the 18th; Maya sends pricing by Tuesday the 17th; security deep-dive scheduling for week of 23rd. Anything else?
[07:37] Omar: If you can include an example of fallback latencies for sequences 128/256/512, that'd be ideal.
[07:42] Lucas: I'll include that.
[07:44] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[07:47] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up in the doc. End call.
[07:50] (meeting ends)
